newsitem.title: PERU: Peru hostage crisis set for marathon haul.
newsitem.headline: Peru hostage crisis set for marathon haul.

text.p: In the battle of wills between the Peruvian government and Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages inside the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima, both sides are gearing up for a potentially marathon siege.
Seven weeks after the dramatic assault on a garden party at the residence on Dec. 17, neither has shifted from its original, intransigent position.
"It's stalemate. Neither side wants to give ground or lose face," said one diplomat in Lima who asked not to be named.
"It's bad news for the hostages because they're going to be in there for a long time yet," he added.
President Alberto Fujimori, who has boasted of using his "oriental patience" to confront the crisis, said in interviews last week that the siege could last weeks or even months.
Fujimori, the son of Japanese immigrants, even raised the example of the 1980 U.S. Embassy crisis in Iran.

"I don't have the faintest idea how long it will be before there is a solution to the crisis. Remember that there was a seizure in Iran that lasted 444 days," he told Argentina's Clarin newspaper in an interview published on Friday.

Though still far short of that drama, the Lima hostage crisis is well on the way to surpassing the 1980 siege at the Dominican Embassy in Colombia, where hostages eventually negotiated their own release with nationalist M-19 guerrillas after 61 days.
When the 15-odd Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas stormed a garden party at the residence and seized more than 500 guests, few thought the siege would last so long.
As the mostly teenage, jungle-trained gunmen watched over a glittering array of VIP hostages, the cramped residence seemed like a powder keg, ready to go off at any moment.
But after an early threat to start killing hostages, the guerrillas have released most of them, hanging on to 72 -- a far more manageable number.
In almost daily broadcasts via megaphone from an upper window of the diplomatic mansion, the rebels insist that they have no intention of giving up their fight.
"We have patience, serenity and all the time in the world ... The ball is in their court," MRTA international spokesman Isaac Velazco said in a recent interview with Reuters from Hamburg.
The two sides have not held direct talks for more than a month and remain deadlocked over the rebels' main demand for the freedom of about 400 jailed comrades.
Following a crisis summit with Japan's Ryutaro Hashimoto in Toronto on Saturday, Fujimori said talks would be resumed but made it clear he had not relaxed his tough line.
"There will be absolutely no release of MRTA prisoners," he told a news conference after a two-hour meeting with Hashimoto.
Nestor Cerpa, the mastermind behind the assault and the highest-ranking MRTA leader not behind bars, issued a stinging and defiant response from inside the residence.
"That signifies that it is the MRTA that has to concede. That will not happen. We will not step back," he told the CBS Telenoticias network in a walkie-talkie interview.
Red Cross officials said they have begun preparing hostages for many more nights under the guns of the heavily armed guerrillas.
Relatives too are being warned not to expect a prompt solution and hot lines manned by psychologists have been set up to provide round-the-clock counselling.

"It's them (the hostages) that the government should be thinking of as the crisis continues. God knows what they and their families must be suffering," said Augusto Carmona, as he peddled cigarettes and chewing gum to journalists and police a block from the residence.
